source.title: Can LLMs facilitate interpretation of pre-trained language models?
source.authors: Basel Mousi; Nadir Durrani; Fahim Dalvi

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports neuron-ranking overlap between broad linguistic categories and their sub-concepts, but does not test whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether such mixtures are common.
record.gate_note: The paper applies Probeless neuron ranking to concepts and reports top-10 neuron overlap between super-concepts and sub-concepts (Table 5). This is a related neuron-analysis result, but it does not measure polysemanticity as defined by any claim version. The human annotation agreement results and probing-classifier accuracies do not measure the claim's subject and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper uses ChatGPT to label clusters of contextual representations and applies Probeless neuron ranking to these concepts. It reports top-10 neuron overlap between a super-concept and its sub-concepts, which are related categories by construction. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common such neurons are, or why they arise. It does not mention polysemanticity at all, so even 'discusses' overstates the link; it neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that ChatGPT gives accurate, semantically richer labels for latent concepts in pre-trained language models: 90.7% were judged acceptable, and 75.5% were equal to or better than human BCN labels. They add that these labels enable fine-grained probing and neuron analysis, including the finding that top neurons for super-concepts are distributed among the top neurons of sub-concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Probeless neuron rankings to analyze concept hierarchies; it does not reproduce a method for testing polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: In fine-tuned BERT-base-cased (POS tagging), top-10 Probeless-ranked neurons for broad POS super-concepts partly overlap with those for their ChatGPT-labelled sub-concepts. Mean overlap is 0.30–0.40 (Table 5), and the paper also gives per-sub-concept scores (Table 11) and name-cluster scores (Table 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons ranked highest for a broad linguistic category are partly shared with the neurons ranked highest for its fine-grained sub-categories.

record.problems: The neuron results are based on ranking overlap, not causal tests or direct examination of neuron responses to unrelated inputs. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these overlap values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 11 gives individual sub-concept overlap scores for the same neuron-ranking analysis. These detailed values are not extracted; Table 5's aggregate alignments are retained, and none of these measurements tests a listed claim version.

untested.parts: All: no measure of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, nor of layer differences.
All: no superposition or capacity analysis.
All: no analysis of initialization, regularization or training noise.
All: no manipulation of activation function, architecture or regularization.
All: overlap is among related sub-concepts by design; no examination of whether mixtures of unrelated inputs are rare.
All: no study of activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The paper does not engage with polysemanticity, and the 'cites_only' label is the closest available fit even though no polysemanticity source is cited. Table 12 (name-cluster overlaps) is not declared in rows_left_out, but it is not relevant to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models and responses to unrelated image inputs.
The share of MLP neurons in transformer language models that respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and layer differences in that share.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemantic-neuron share and performance.
Whether apparently polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job, and whether unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether polysemanticity depends on activation range examined or explanation-scoring method.
